book_title: Madhya Pradesh District Gazetteers: Vidisha — Government of Madhya Pradesh
quote: The puranas mention Vindhyasakti (c. A.D. 255-275), the founder of the dynasty, as a ruler of Vidisha. Vindhyasakti seems to have enlarged his patrimony, comprising a district or two in Vidarbha, and extended its limits across the Vindhya range, so as to include a portion of Malwa. This may perhaps explain why the puranas mention Vindhyasakti as the ruler of Vidisha.\( ^{4} \)
note: Vindhyasakti of the Vakatakas mentioned in the puranas as ruler of Vidisha.
author: Government of Madhya Pradesh

book_title: Madhya Pradesh District Gazetteers: Vidisha — Government of Madhya Pradesh
quote: Chandragupta II left undisputed evidence of his sovereignty in Malwa in the shape of two epigraphs at the caves of the Udayagiri hills of Vidisha. These record the gift made by the feudatory ruler Maharaja Sanakanika during the reign of Chandragupta II in 82 Gupta Era (A.D. 401); and the excavation of a cave by his minister of peace and war, Virasena, who came to this place with the king himself.
note: Two Chandragupta II epigraphs at the Udayagiri caves of Vidisha (Gupta Era 82).
author: Government of Madhya Pradesh

book_title: Madhya Pradesh District Gazetteers: Vidisha — Government of Madhya Pradesh
quote: The poet Kalidasa, who probably adorned the court of this monarch with 8 other jewels (raina), has immortalised the grandeur and beauty of Vidisha and its environs in his famous work Meghaduta.
note: Kalidasa's Meghaduta on Vidisha and its environs.
author: Government of Madhya Pradesh

book_title: Madhya Pradesh District Gazetteers: Vidisha — Government of Madhya Pradesh
quote: The early Kalachuris, who claimed their descent from the Haihaya king Kartaviryarjuna and grew powerful in northern Maharashtra, Gujarat and in parts of Malwa during the later part of the 6th century A. D. became the rulers of Vidisha. They used the Kalachuri Era. There are epigraphic records of three of these rulers, viz. Krishnaraja, his son Sankaragana and grandson Buddharaja. All of them were devotees of Siva.
note: Early Kalachuris became rulers of Vidisha; Krishnaraja, Sankaragana, Buddharaja.
author: Government of Madhya Pradesh

book_title: Madhya Pradesh District Gazetteers: Vidisha — Government of Madhya Pradesh
quote: His Vadner grant dated K. E. 360 (A. D. 608) was issued from Vaidisa (Vidisha or Besnagar), in order to grant land in the Vatanagara bhoga (Vadner in the Chander taluk of Nasik district). It is not unlikely that East Malwa, of which Vidisha was the old capital, was conquered by one of these kings from Devagupta of the Later Gupta dynasty.
note: Buddharaja's Vadner grant of 608 issued from Vaidisa.
author: Government of Madhya Pradesh

book_title: Madhya Pradesh District Gazetteers: Vidisha — Government of Madhya Pradesh
quote: But the Muslim traveller had admitted that the Hindus had always called it Bhilsa ever since its foundation Bhilsa is a corrupt form of Bhailasvamin or Bhailasvamo, that was originally the name of an idol of the Sun god, enshrined and worshipped in a great temple of this place. An inscription from Vidisha, incised during the rule of king Krishna (probably the Rashtrakuta monarch Krishna III of A. D. 939-68), refers to this temple of Bhillasvamin.
note: Bhilsa from Bhailasvamin, sun-god idol temple; inscription under Krishna III.
author: Government of Madhya Pradesh

book_title: Madhya Pradesh District Gazetteers: Vidisha — Government of Madhya Pradesh
quote: During the 10th century A. D., however, it was incorporated in the Chandella empire. It is said that the most powerful monarch of this family, namely, Dhanga (A. D. 954-1002) extended his kingdom upto the Jamuna (Kalandi) in the north, Gwalior (Gopa mountain) in the north-west and Bhasvat on the river Malwa (Bhilsa or Vidisha on the Betwa).
note: Vidisha incorporated in the Chandella empire under Dhanga.
author: Government of Madhya Pradesh

book_title: Madhya Pradesh District Gazetteers: Vidisha — Government of Madhya Pradesh
quote: \( ^{2} \)  This image is ascribed to the age of Chandragupta II (A. D. 5th century). Its size and height are such as to suit the abacus top of Kham Baba pillar. Probably this Gupta King, being a staunch devotee of Vishnu, crowned the column with this image of Garuda.
note: Garuda image ascribed to age of Chandragupta II, 5th century, probably crowning the Kham Baba pillar.
author: Government of Madhya Pradesh

book_title: Madhya Pradesh District Gazetteers: Vidisha — Government of Madhya Pradesh
quote: It is in eight lines. It is dated in the year 106 of the Gupta Era, corresponding to A. D. 272.
note: Udayagiri cave 20 (Parshvanatha) near Vidisha: eight-line inscription dated Gupta Era 106, A.D. 272.
author: Government of Madhya Pradesh

book_title: Madhya Pradesh District Gazetteers: Vidisha — Government of Madhya Pradesh
quote:
On the back wall of it there is an inscription of five lines,
indicating that the cave was made by a minister of Chandragupta. The roof inside is ornamented with a large lotus flower. The inscription informs that the minister accompanied the king and made this cave, dedicated to Shambhu or Siva. Unfortunately the inscription is not dated.
note: Tawa cave inscription: cave made by a minister of Chandragupta, dedicated to Shambhu or Siva; inscription undated.
author: Government of Madhya Pradesh

book_title: Madhya Pradesh District Gazetteers: Vidisha — Government of Madhya Pradesh
quote:
Both these contain important historical inscriptions of the Gupta period. The cave No. 6
inscriptions bears inscription of Chandragupta II dated in the year 82 of the Gupta Era.
note: Udayagiri caves 6 and 7 contain Gupta-period inscriptions; cave 6 bears an inscription of Chandragupta II dated Gupta Era 82.
author: Government of Madhya Pradesh

book_title: Madhya Pradesh District Gazetteers: Vidisha — Government of Madhya Pradesh
quote: It was a rich and prosperous trading centre in ancient period. The economic prosperity of this area was retained at least till the days of the Imperial Guptas, for in his Meghaduta, Kalidasa has referred to Vidisha as a place where everybody gets wealth to his heart's content. This economic prosperity was due to its advantageous position on the cross-roads of two important trade routes. One of these connected Mathura with Pratisthan (modern Paithan on the Godavari) via-Vidisha and another route, passing through this place, connected Pataliputra in the east with Bharukachchha (modern Broach), in the west.
note: Vidisha as a rich trading centre on the cross-roads of two trade routes (Mathura to Pratisthan; Pataliputra to Bharukachchha), with Kalidasa's Meghaduta reference.
author: Government of Madhya Pradesh

book_title: Madhya Pradesh District Gazetteers: Vidisha — Government of Madhya Pradesh
quote: The economic prosperity was due to its advantageous position on the cross roads of two important trade routes. One of these ran from Pratisthan (modern Paithan in the Godavari region) to Mahishmati, Ujjayini, Gonadda, Vaidisa (Vidisha) and Kausambi, while the other connected Bharukachchha (Broach) and Surparak on the Arbian Sea, to Mathura via Ujjayini. A branch of this route ran from Vidisha to Kausambi through the valley of the Betwa, or Betravati and then to Pataliputra.\(^{1}\)
note: Vidisha's prosperity from cross-roads of two trade routes, including a branch through the Betwa valley.
author: Government of Madhya Pradesh

book_title: Madhya Pradesh District Gazetteers: Vidisha — Government of Madhya Pradesh
quote: Malwa, to which the present District of Vidisha belongs, had been a centre of culture and civilization for centuries. The roads that passed through Malwa were military as well as trade routes. The commercial activities of this region received an added impetus from these routes.
note: Malwa, to which Vidisha District belongs, a centre of culture for centuries; roads were military as well as trade routes that spurred commerce.
author: Government of Madhya Pradesh

book_title: Madhya Pradesh District Gazetteers: Vidisha — Government of Madhya Pradesh
quote: In the ancient period, the District lay on the important road link connecting Northern India with Southern India and the Magadha empire with part of Surparaka. The earliest Buddhist Literature records the trade route of Paithana in the Deccan to Sravasthi, \( ^{1} \) passing through the District.
note: In the ancient period the District lay on the road link connecting Northern and Southern India; earliest Buddhist literature records the Paithana to Sravasthi trade route passing through it.
author: Government of Madhya Pradesh

book_title: Madhya Pradesh District Gazetteers: Vidisha — Government of Madhya Pradesh
quote: The Skanda Purana refers to Vidisha as a tirth (holy place) which should be visited after visiting Someshwar.
note: Skanda Purana refers to Vidisha as a tirth to be visited after Someshwar
author: Government of Madhya Pradesh

book_title: The Cultural Heritage of Madhya Bharat — Patil, D. R.
quote:
The Haihayas later separated into a number of branches one of which ruled at Vidisha (Bhilsa) which in Central India is next only to Mahishmati inthe

point of its high antiquity.
note: A branch of the Haihayas ruled at Vidisha (Bhilsa), which is next only to Mahishmati in antiquity in Central India.
author: Patil, D. R.

book_title: The Cultural Heritage of Madhya Bharat — Patil, D. R.
quote:
Prince Ashoka had married a daughter of a banker of Vidisha from whom were born prince Mahendra and princess Sanghamitra so famous in the history of early Buddhism.
The services rendered by Ashoka to the cause and spread of Buddhism need hardly be mentioned. He laid the foundations of the great Stupa at Sanchi and raised a huge monolithic pillar close to it with his usual edicts inscribed thereon.
note: Prince Ashoka married a daughter of a Vidisha banker; he laid the foundations of the Sanchi stupa and raised a monolithic pillar close to it.
author: Patil, D. R.

book_title: The Cultural Heritage of Madhya Bharat — Patil, D. R.
quote:
We learn from Kalidasa's literary romance: Malavikagnimitra that the crown prince Agnimitra served as a Viceroy at Vidisha during the reign of his father Pushyamitra. That Vidisha was within Shunga dominion is further supported by the Besnagar Pillar inscription of Heliodoros. It is a Garuda pillar set up by him during his stay there. He is mentioned therein as having come as the ambassador of the Indo-Greek King Antialcidas of Taxila to the court of King Bhagabhadra. This Bhagabhadra is generally identified with the fifth Shunga king Bhandaka of the later Shungas who are supposed to have made Vidisha their capital.
It is interesting to find from the inscription that the Greek ambassador had embraced the Bhagavata sect and raised the pillar in honour of the god Vasudeva, an event of much significance to the history of the Bhagavata sect in India.
note: Agnimitra as viceroy at Vidisha (Malavikagnimitra); Heliodoros Garuda pillar at Besnagar as ambassador of Antialcidas to Bhagabhadra, embracing the Bhagavata sect.
author: Patil, D. R.

book_title: The Cultural Heritage of Madhya Bharat — Patil, D. R.
quote: It seems that in the midst of the rapid spread of Buddhism in the country Vidisha was holding out as a centre of the orthodox faith as testified not only by the inscription but by a number of other antiquities found here belonging to the succeeding centuries. In any case it is quite clear that the Vidisha of the Shungas, and of the succeeding dynasties, was a centre of a great cultural and art movement now represented by the surviving monuments in the neighbourhood of Bhilsa and Sanchi which rank high amongst the most remarkable and extensive of the remains to be found in the whole of India.
note: Vidisha as a centre of orthodox faith and of a great cultural and art movement represented by monuments near Bhilsa and Sanchi.
author: Patil, D. R.

book_title: The Cultural Heritage of Madhya Bharat — Patil, D. R.
quote:
*More than a dozen images of the Saptamatrikas. Durga, Kubera, etc., have been recovered from Besnagar which would seem to belong to the age of the Nagas rather than the Guptas to which they have so far been assigned.
†A chief of this tribe mentioned as Maharaja was ruling as a vassal of Chandragupta II near Udyagiri (Bhilsa) where he caused a cave to be excavated.
note: Footnote: more than a dozen images of Saptamatrikas, Durga, Kubera recovered from Besnagar; and a Sanakanika Maharaja vassal of Chandragupta II excavated a cave near Udayagiri (Bhilsa).
author: Patil, D. R.

book_title: The Cultural Heritage of Madhya Bharat — Patil, D. R.
quote: The antiquities from Besnagar are most important for the early history of the Hindu sects of Vaishnavism and Shaivism. The colossal image of Durga, the sculptures of the Seven Mothers, Nrisimha, Vishnu and the Ekamukha lingas are the instances in point, in addition to the stone figures of Kubera and other antiquities.
note: Besnagar antiquities important for early Vaishnavism and Shaivism: colossal Durga, Seven Mothers, Nrisimha, Vishnu, Ekamukha lingas.
author: Patil, D. R.

book_title: The Cultural Heritage of Madhya Bharat — Patil, D. R.
quote: It is possible that just at this time a Vaishnava temple existed at Besnagar, in front of which a Greek ambassador erected the famous Garudadhvaja still standing in situ. But nothing has survived to show how the earliest Hindu sanctuaries, if any, were in those days.
note: A Vaishnava temple possibly existed at Besnagar in front of which the Greek ambassador erected the Garudadhvaja; nothing survives of earliest Hindu sanctuaries.
author: Patil, D. R.

book_title: The Cultural Heritage of Madhya Bharat — Patil, D. R.
quote: There is, however, a group of antiquities, viz. the free standing colossal statues, with regard to the age of which there is a divergence of opinions assigning them from the pre-Mauryan to the Shunga times. For such statues the ancient site of Besnagar may take the place of pride in yielding, up-to-date, three exactly similar figures of Yakshini* and, what may be considered to be, the most unique and gainly figure of Kubera recovered from the river Betwa a few months back.
note: Besnagar yielded three similar Yakshini figures and a Kubera figure recovered from the Betwa, free-standing colossal statues of disputed date (pre-Mauryan to Shunga).
author: Patil, D. R.

book_title: The Cultural Heritage of Madhya Bharat — Patil, D. R.
quote: The latter site has also yielded a little less than a dozen statues of the Seven Mothers, Durga, Nrisimha, Kubera, etc., all free-standing and carved on four sides, which artistically should be taken to form a joining link between the earlier art and the classical art of the Gupta period. In the matters of form, volume and expression they somewhat differ from their earlier counterparts, bringing them much closer to the classic art of the later age.
note: Besnagar yielded a little under a dozen free-standing statues of the Seven Mothers, Durga, Nrisimha, Kubera, a link between earlier art and Gupta classic art.
author: Patil, D. R.

book_title: The Cultural Heritage of Madhya Bharat — Patil, D. R.
quote: It will be seen from above that from the view-point of antiquity and historical importance Bhilsa is the richest district in Madhya Bharat. The monuments here are mostly centred round the ancient city site of Vidisha, i. e., at Besnagar and Udaygiri, a mile to the west.
note: Bhilsa the richest district in antiquity and historical importance; its monuments centred round ancient Vidisha at Besnagar and Udaygiri.
author: Patil, D. R.

book_title: The Cultural Heritage of Madhya Bharat — Patil, D. R.
quote: Though Vidisha was a great centre of the orthodox religion, under the Shungas and later, the popularity of the new faith is amply reflected in the monuments of Sanchi and Besnagar, as at Ujjain and Kasrawad. There were, however, no great monarchs ruling in Madhya Bharat who had special attachment for the faith with the result that little of recorded or literary evidence is available to attest to the extent and popularity of Buddhism then in Madhya Bharat. Under the Guptas, it appears, Vidisha was a stronghold of Brahminism and at other places also Buddhism was losing ground.
note: Vidisha a great centre of orthodox religion under the Shungas and later, while Buddhism is reflected in Sanchi and Besnagar monuments; under the Guptas Vidisha a stronghold of Brahminism.
author: Patil, D. R.

book_title: The Cultural Heritage of Madhya Bharat — Patil, D. R.
quote: in Madhya Bharat is found in the stone images of Durga and of the Seven Mothers and the Ekamukha Lingas from Besnagar now in the Gwalior Museum. They have been dated to the early Gupta period of the 4th century A.D. though as observed elsewhere their date can be pushed back to a century.
note: Earliest evidence of Shaivism in Madhya Bharat: Durga, Seven Mothers and Ekamukha Lingas from Besnagar, dated to the early Gupta period (4th century A.D.).
author: Patil, D. R.

book_title: The Cultural Heritage of Madhya Bharat — Patil, D. R.
quote: Vaishnavism.—Archaeologically Vaishnavism is the earliest recorded sect in Madhya Bharat as is evident from the famous Heliodoros pillar inscription of 1st or 2nd century B.C. at Besnagar near Bhilsa. The inscription states that a Greek ambassador from Taxila at the court of the Shunga King of Vidisha (Bhilsa) had become a convert to the Bhagavata sect and raised a Garuda pillar in honour of the god Vasudeva.
note: Heliodoros pillar inscription of 1st or 2nd century B.C. at Besnagar: a Greek ambassador from Taxila at the Shunga king's court at Vidisha became a Bhagavata and raised a Garuda pillar to Vasudeva.
author: Patil, D. R.

book_title: The Cultural Heritage of Madhya Bharat — Patil, D. R.
quote: Bhilsa is the modern representative of the ancient Vidisha which stood on the other side of the river Betwa 2 miles to the north. The name of Bhilsa is not directly related to the ancient name of Vidisha; it seems to have been derived from a great temple of the sun god called as Bhailasvamin and an incidental reference to the place as Mahabalistan is made by Albiruni in the early 11th century A. D.
note: Bhilsa is the modern representative of ancient Vidisha, which stood across the Betwa 2 miles to the north; name said to derive from a sun temple Bhailasvamin.
author: Patil, D. R.

book_title: The Cultural Heritage of Madhya Bharat — Patil, D. R.
quote:
Site of Besnagar.—The site of the famous ancient city, mentioned as Vessanagar in the Pali books of the Buddhists and by the name of Vidisha in the Sanskrit literature of the Hindus, is about two miles to the west of the Bhilsa Railway Station and

is situated in the fork of the two rivers, the Betwa (Vetravati) and the Bes. In the days of the Buddha Vidisha was a great centre of trade connecting the flourishing towns of the Gangetic plains with the western coast and the Deccan. It came more into prominence in the time of Ashoka, the Mauryan Emperor, who had married a daughter of a merchant from the town. Under the Shungas it was a great religious centre, for Hindus and Buddhists alike, as is amply reflected in the famous ruins of Sanchi close by and in the numerous Hindu antiquities found from its old site.
note: Besnagar (Vessanagar/Vidisha) in the fork of the Betwa and the Bes; a trade centre in the days of the Buddha; under Ashoka and the Shungas a religious centre.
author: Patil, D. R.

book_title: The Cultural Heritage of Madhya Bharat — Patil, D. R.
quote: Of them the three free-standing statues of Yakshinis, a colossal statue of Kubera, the images of Durga, Seven Mothers, Nrisimha, etc., are the most interesting, most of them being now preserved in the Museum at Gwalior. On the site itself now stands a monolithic pillar known in the locality by the name of Kham Baba, "the Pillar God". The pillar bears a Brahmi inscription stating that it was set up as Garuda pillar in honour of God Vasudeva (Vishnu) by a Greek named Heliodoros who had come to the court of King Bhagabhadra of Vidisha as an ambassador from the Greek king Antialcidas of Takshashila (Taxila) in Western Punjab and who has styled himself as a Bhagavata, having been a convert to Hinduism.
note: Besnagar finds (Yakshinis, Kubera, Durga, Seven Mothers); Kham Baba pillar with Brahmi inscription of Heliodoros, ambassador of Antialcidas to King Bhagabhadra, styling himself a Bhagavata.
author: Patil, D. R.

book_title: The Cultural Heritage of Madhya Bharat — Patil, D. R.
quote:
Till the age of the Guptas (5th century A. D.) it was a prosperous town but what happened to it afterwards is not known; for by the 10th century the town of Bhilsa, on the other side of the river, had already came into existence, the older town having been almost totally deserted by then.
The site of the ancient town is now marked by mounds which have from time to time yielded numerous stone or other antiquities of historical or artistic importance.
note: Prosperous until the Gupta age; by the 10th century Bhilsa on the other side of the river had arisen and the older town was almost deserted; site now marked by mounds.
author: Patil, D. R.

book_title: The Cultural Heritage of Madhya Bharat — Patil, D. R.
quote: In ancient geography it was called as Dasharna known as such from the days of the Buddha to those of Kalidasa in about the 5th century. A. D. The name still lives in the modern name of a stream called Dashan which, rising in the Bhopal territory and flowing through Bundelkhand, empties into the river Betwa. In late historical times it came to be known as part of the Gondwada ruled by the semi-civilized tribe of the Gonds. The ancient Vidisha and its later representative Bhilsa had always been the focal point of this region.
note: Region called Dasharna in ancient geography; the name survives in the Dashan stream flowing into the Betwa; ancient Vidisha and later Bhilsa the focal point.
author: Patil, D. R.

book_title: The Cultural Heritage of Madhya Bharat — Patil, D. R.
quote: According to his Nasik prashasti, territories which he conquered from Nahapana included Anupa (the country on the Narbada about Nimar), Akara (east Malwa) and Avanti (west Malwa).
note: Nasik prashasti of Gautamiputra lists Anupa, Akara (east Malwa) and Avanti (west Malwa) among his conquests.
author: Patil, D. R.

book_title: The Cultural Heritage of Madhya Bharat — Patil, D. R.
quote: According to a passage in Puranas, they were a people known as Andhras led by the then ruler Simuka, generally identified with the Simuka Satavahana of the Nanaghat inscription. Simuka, in the course of his northern campaigns when he extirpated the last Shunga and Kanvas, must have conquered districts round Vidisha. For, besides the Puranic passage, discovery of certain early Satavahana coins suggests that the Malwa region was within early Satavahana influence.
note: Simuka Satavahana is said to have conquered districts round Vidisha; early Satavahana coins suggest Malwa within their influence.
author: Patil, D. R.

book_title: The Cultural Heritage of Madhya Bharat — Patil, D. R.
quote: While the southern parts of Madhya Bharat were thus undergoing rapid political changes the regions about Gwalior and Bhilsa were under a comparably more stable government of the Nagas ruling in small principalities from Kantipui (according to Cunningham Kotwal 20 miles north of Gwalior) Padmavati (Pawaya, 40 miles south of Gwalior) and Vidisha (Bhilsa). Numerous copper cast coins of the Nagas have been found at Kotwal and Pawaya which testify to this.
note: Regions about Gwalior and Bhilsa under the Nagas, ruling from Kantipuri, Padmavati and Vidisha; copper coins found at Kotwal and Pawaya.
author: Patil, D. R.

book_title: The Cultural Heritage of Madhya Bharat — Patil, D. R.
quote: In the north about Gwalior the authority of the Nagas was supplanted by the newly rising power of the Guptas and as stated in his famous Allahabad Pillar Inscription Samudragupta finally vanquished them sometime in the middle of the 4th century A. D. The inscription also claims victory over a number of ruling tribes and dynasties in Northern India such as the Malavas mentioned above and the Sanakanikas† of the region near Bhilsa. It seems therefore fairly clear that under the Guptas the whole of Madhya Bharat was once more under one sceptre with an assured peace and a stable government in power.
note: Samudragupta's Allahabad Pillar Inscription claims victory over the Nagas and the Sanakanikas near Bhilsa; Madhya Bharat under one sceptre under the Guptas.
author: Patil, D. R.

book_title: The Cultural Heritage of Madhya Bharat — Patil, D. R.
quote: The prosperity of Madhya Bharat territories under the Guptas is well reflected in the few monuments left at Pawaya, Tumain (Guna District), Besnagar and Udaygiri (Bhilsa), Mandsor and in the famous caves and paintings of Bagh. The antiquities recovered from the sites of Padmavati (Pawaya) and Vidisha (Besnagar) are unique in the whole range of the classic art of the “Golden Age” of the Guptas.
note: Prosperity under the Guptas reflected in monuments at Besnagar and Udaygiri (Bhilsa); Besnagar antiquities unique in Gupta classic art.
author: Patil, D. R.

book_title: The Cultural Heritage of Madhya Bharat — Patil, D. R.
quote:
The plain of Nimar and eastern part of the plateau near Bhilsa were, however, for a time under the rule of the Rastrakutas* of the
*The Pathari (Bhilsa District) Pillar inscription refers to the erection of the pillar by a Minister of Rastrakuta king Parabala in 861 A. D.
note: Eastern plateau near Bhilsa for a time under the Rastrakutas; Pathari pillar inscription of 861 A.D. records a pillar erected by a minister of Parabala.
author: Patil, D. R.

book_title: The Cultural Heritage of Madhya Bharat — Patil, D. R.
quote:
The caves at Udaygiri.—There are in all 20 caves excavated on the eastern face of the Udaygiri hill. The caves are mostly small rock-cut chambers enshrining idols or images of divinities carved into the rock of the hill, Caves Nos. 1 and 20 are Jain caves. Architecturally cave No. 1 is a little interesting in so far as it represents the earliest phase in the development of temple architecture in India, planned as it is with a small

shrine and a simple porch in front.
note: Twenty caves on the eastern face of Udaygiri hill; Cave 1 (Jain) represents the earliest phase of temple architecture with a small shrine and simple porch.
author: Patil, D. R.

book_title: The Cultural Heritage of Madhya Bharat — Patil, D. R.
quote: Of the other caves, the most notable are the caves Nos. 6 and 7 containing important historical inscriptions of the Gupta period, and No. 13 for the large rock-cut image of Sheshashayi Vishnu in it.
note: Caves 6 and 7 contain important historical inscriptions of the Gupta period; Cave 13 a Sheshashayi Vishnu.
author: Patil, D. R.

book_title: The Cultural Heritage of Madhya Bharat — Patil, D. R.
quote: Sarais, Bridges and Dharmashalas.—Being placed in the central parts of the country the territory of Madhya Bharat must have been called upon to respond to the normal needs of trade and commerce by maintaining an effective line of communications consistent with the conditions of the times. The great trade routes connecting the northern and southern parts of the country inevitably passed through this region. In ancient times Vidisha (Bhilsa), Ujjain and Mahishmati formed the important links joining the western coast, the Gangetic plains and the Deccan.
note: Trade routes connecting north and south passed through Madhya Bharat; in ancient times Vidisha (Bhilsa), Ujjain and Mahishmati joined the western coast, the Gangetic plains and the Deccan.
author: Patil, D. R.

book_title: कथा उदयपुर (Jagta Hua Kasba) — Hindi original
quote:
विदिशा का ज्ञात इतिहास ढाई हजार साल का है। एक लंबी समृद्ध सांस्कृतिक परंपरा है, लेकिन आज के समाज में उसका लेशमात्र नहीं है।
*Gloss [my translation]:* The known history of Vidisha is two and a half thousand years old. It has a long, rich cultural tradition, but today's society retains not a trace of it.
note: States Vidisha's known history is two and a half thousand years old, a long rich cultural tradition.
gloss: The known history of Vidisha is two and a half thousand years old. It has a long, rich cultural tradition, but today's society retains not a trace of it.

book_title: कथा उदयपुर (Jagta Hua Kasba) — Hindi original
quote:
अब हम उदयपुर के जिला मुख्यालय पर जा पहुँचे थे, जो ऐतिहासिक रूप से उदयपुर से भी काफी पहले से समृद्ध प्रमुख नगर रहा है। विदिशा का अतीत सम्राट अशोक तक तो सीधा ही ले जाता है, जिनका विवाह यहीं की एक कन्या से हुआ था। 23 सौ साल पहले।
*Gloss [my translation]:* We had reached the district headquarters, historically a prosperous major city much earlier than Udaipur. Vidisha's past leads straight to Emperor Ashoka, who married a girl from here, 2300 years ago.
note: Vidisha described as a prosperous major town long before Udaypur; its past leads straight to Ashoka, married to a local woman 2300 years ago.
gloss: We had reached the district headquarters, historically a prosperous major city much earlier than Udaipur. Vidisha's past leads straight to Emperor Ashoka, who married a girl from here, 2300 years ago.

book_title: कथा उदयपुर (Jagta Hua Kasba) — Hindi original
quote:
विदिशा उदयपुर की तुलना में बड़ा और अधिक प्राचीन शहर था, जिसका ज्ञात इतिहास ही मौर्ष्य तक तो बड़े आराम से ले जाता है। मौर्ष्य साम्राज्य में अशोक सम्राट बनने के पहले उज्जैन में रहे थे। विदिशा के पास सांची के स्तूप तभी बनना शुरू हुए थे। कालिदास के मेघदूत विदिशा की आकाशीय यात्रा करते हुए दिखाई दिए हैं। बीच में गुप्त काल गुजरा, जिसके प्रमाण इस इलाके में जगह-जगह बिखरे हुए हैं।
*Gloss [my translation]:* Vidisha was a bigger and more ancient city than Udaipur, whose known history goes back easily to the Mauryas. Ashoka lived in Ujjain before becoming emperor. The Sanchi stupas near Vidisha began to be built then. Kalidasa's clouds travel through Vidisha in the Meghaduta. Then came the Gupta period, whose evidence is scattered around the region.
note: Vidisha larger and older than Udaypur, known history reaching Mauryas; Sanchi stupas, Kalidasa's Meghaduta and Gupta remains.
gloss: Vidisha was a bigger and more ancient city than Udaipur, whose known history goes back easily to the Mauryas. Ashoka lived in Ujjain before becoming emperor. The Sanchi stupas near Vidisha began to be built then. Kalidasa's clouds travel through Vidisha in the Meghaduta. Then came the Gupta period, whose evidence is scattered around the region.

book_title: कथा उदयपुर (Jagta Hua Kasba) — Hindi original
quote:
यह एक ऐसे शहर की यादगार यात्रा थी, जहां दो हज़ार साल पहले एक यूनानी राजदूत आया था। उसने विदिशा आकर यहां के समाज और रीति-रिवाजों के असर में वैष्णव धर्म स्वीकार करने का निर्णय ले लिया था। वह इतिहास में दर्ज विदिशा के लिए गर्व करने लायक एक अमर प्रसंग है, जिसकी याद बेतवा नदी के किनारे पत्थर के एक स्तंभ में दर्ज है। वह स्तंभ खामबाबा के नाम से प्रसिद्ध है, जो कभी एक मंदिर के सामने गढ़ स्तंभ की शक्ल में स्थापित किया गया होगा। आज मंदिर का नामोनिशान बाकी नहीं है। लेकिन हेलिओडोरस का वह लेख आज भी उस स्तंभ पर पढ़ा जा सकता है।
*Gloss [my translation]:* It was a memorable visit to a city where two thousand years ago a Greek ambassador came. Moved by the society and customs, he decided to accept Vaishnavism. It is an immortal episode recorded on a stone pillar on the Betwa, famed as Khambaba, once a garuda pillar before a temple. No trace of the temple remains, but Heliodorus's inscription can still be read on the pillar.
note: Heliodorus's visit to Vidisha and conversion to Vaishnavism, recorded on the Khambaba pillar by the Betwa.
gloss: It was a memorable visit to a city where two thousand years ago a Greek ambassador came. Moved by the society and customs, he decided to accept Vaishnavism. It is an immortal episode recorded on a stone pillar on the Betwa, famed as Khambaba, once a garuda pillar before a temple. No trace of the temple remains, but Heliodorus's inscription can still be read on the pillar.

book_title: कथा उदयपुर (Jagta Hua Kasba) — Hindi original
quote:
जब वह पहली बार यहां आया था तब मगध सम्राट अशोक और पुण्यमित्र शुंग के किस्से बहुत ताजे थे। सांची में स्तूपों का निर्माण जारी था। महेंद्र और संघमित्रा श्रीलंका प्रस्थान के पहले अपनी माता से मिलने आए थे। शुंगों की यज्ञवेदियों के धुएं की सुगंध हवाओं को ताजादम बनाए हुए थे।
*Gloss [my translation]:* When he first came, the stories of Magadha's Emperor Ashoka and Pushyamitra Shunga were very fresh. Stupas were still being built at Sanchi. Mahendra and Sanghamitra had come to meet their mother before leaving for Sri Lanka. The fragrance of the smoke of the Shungas' sacrificial altars freshened the air.
note: Imagined account of Heliodorus's time: Ashoka and Pushyamitra Shunga stories fresh, Sanchi stupas under construction, Mahendra and Sanghamitra visiting their mother.
gloss: When he first came, the stories of Magadha's Emperor Ashoka and Pushyamitra Shunga were very fresh. Stupas were still being built at Sanchi. Mahendra and Sanghamitra had come to meet their mother before leaving for Sri Lanka. The fragrance of the smoke of the Shungas' sacrificial altars freshened the air.

book_title: कथा उदयपुर (Jagta Hua Kasba) — Hindi original
quote:
वह भी विदिशा को दिल दे बैठा। इतना कि उसने अपना धर्म ही बदल लिया। इसकी विधिवत घोषणा एक बड़े स्तंभ पर अंकित करा दी थी ताकि इतिहास को भलीभांति पता रहे।
*Gloss [my translation]:* He gave his heart to Vidisha so much that he changed his religion. He had it formally announced inscribed on a large pillar so that history would know it well.
note: Heliodorus changed his religion and had it announced on a large pillar.
gloss: He gave his heart to Vidisha so much that he changed his religion. He had it formally announced inscribed on a large pillar so that history would know it well.

book_title: कथा उदयपुर (Jagta Hua Kasba) — Hindi original
quote:
आज का मालवा ईसा पूर्व की सदियों में दशाणर्ण और अवन्ति दो नामों से जाना जाता था। यह विशाल क्षेत्र सम्मिलित तौर पर अशोक के अधीन था। बाद में इसे मालवा कहा जाने लगा। विदिशा पूर्वी मालवा का केन्द्र था और उज्जयिनी पश्चिमी मालवा का।
*Gloss [my translation]:* Today's Malwa was known in the centuries BCE by two names, Dasharna and Avanti. This vast region was jointly under Ashoka. Later it came to be called Malwa. Vidisha was the centre of eastern Malwa and Ujjayini of western Malwa.
note: States that Malwa was known in the centuries BCE as Dasharna and Avanti, jointly under Ashoka, with Vidisha centre of eastern Malwa and Ujjayini of western Malwa.
gloss: Today's Malwa was known in the centuries BCE by two names, Dasharna and Avanti. This vast region was jointly under Ashoka. Later it came to be called Malwa. Vidisha was the centre of eastern Malwa and Ujjayini of western Malwa.

book_title: कथा उदयपुर (Jagta Hua Kasba) — Hindi original
quote:
उस विशाल चट्टान पर विष्णु को पहचानकर उसे कुछ राहत महसूस हुई। विष्णु अपनी भव्य मुद्रा में कमर पर हाथ रखकर वाराह अवतार में शान से खड़े हैं। पृथ्वी स्त्री के रूप में उनकी दाढ़ पर है। विष्णु ने प्रलय में डूबी पृथ्वी का उद्धार किया है। अपने आराध्य विष्णु का यह आशाजनक दृश्य वह अपलक देख रहा है। उदयगिरि में पत्थर पर अंकित 1500 साल पुरानी गुप्त सम्राटों की पवित्र निशानी।
*Gloss [my translation]:* Recognising Vishnu on that huge rock gave him relief. Vishnu stands proudly in his boar incarnation, hand on waist, Earth as a woman on his tusk; Vishnu has rescued the earth sunk in the deluge. A 1500-year-old sacred sign of the Gupta emperors in stone at Udayagiri.
note: Boar-incarnation Vishnu on the Udayagiri rock, a 1500-year-old Gupta emperors' sacred mark.
gloss: Recognising Vishnu on that huge rock gave him relief. Vishnu stands proudly in his boar incarnation, hand on waist, Earth as a woman on his tusk; Vishnu has rescued the earth sunk in the deluge. A 1500-year-old sacred sign of the Gupta emperors in stone at Udayagiri.

book_title: कथा उदयपुर (Jagta Hua Kasba) — Hindi original
quote:
एक बार मेरा जाना एक ऐसी जगह पर हुआ, जो पटारी की तरफ उदयपुर से करीब 15 किलोमीटर एक सुरम्य हरी-भरी पहाड़ियों में है। अगर आप गूगल मैप पर उदयपुर को पटारी से जोड़ेंगे तो ठीक बीच में यह जगह है। पटारी के खंडहरों से साफ पता चलता है कि यह मौय्यों और गुप्त राजाओं के समय एक विकसित नगर रहा होगा।
*Gloss [my translation]:* Once I went to a place about 15 km from Udaypur towards Patari, in picturesque green hills. If you join Udaypur and Patari on Google Maps, this place lies right in the middle. The ruins of Patari clearly show that it must have been a developed town in the time of the Mauryas and Gupta kings.
note: Patari, about 15 km from Udaypur and midway between them on Google Maps, has ruins suggesting a developed town in Mauryan and Gupta times.
gloss: Once I went to a place about 15 km from Udaypur towards Patari, in picturesque green hills. If you join Udaypur and Patari on Google Maps, this place lies right in the middle. The ruins of Patari clearly show that it must have been a developed town in the time of the Mauryas and Gupta kings.

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras — Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
quote: It is interesting to note that the earliest mention of this name is in an inscription of V.S. 935 or 878 A.C. and also that the name figures as Bhillasvāmipura in the Māndhātā inscription of Jayasinha II issued in (V.) S. 1331.
note: Earliest mention of the name Bhillasvāmin is in an inscription of V.S. 935 or 878 A.C.; also Bhillasvāmipura in the Māndhātā inscription of V.S. 1331.
author: Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras — Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
quote: Bhāillasvāmippura (l. 9) is the ancient city of Vidishā (Bhilsā), which was formerly the capital of the Akara-janapada, roughly corresponding to east Mālava. The name Bhillasvāmin (Bhāillasāmin) was originally of an image of the Sun deity worshipped in a temple at that place which subsequently became famous under the deity's name, as we also know from Albērūnī (c. 1030 A.C.) who tells us that “the name of the town is identical with that of the idol worshipped there”.
note: Bhāillasvāmippura is the ancient city of Vidishā (Bhilsā), formerly capital of the Akara-janapada, roughly east Mālava; named from a Sun image, with Albērūnī (c. 1030 A.C.) quoted.
author: Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras — Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
quote: Now, in view of the fact that the Chandēlla territory then extended up to Vidishā in the south-west, the principality of the ruler who is stated to have been placed on the throne by Vāchaspati should be looked for still further in the south or south-west of Vidishā.
note: The Chandēlla territory is said to have then extended up to Vidishā in the south-west.
author: Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras — Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
quote: This suggestion is confirmed by Tale No. 8 of the S.M.K., which states that Pūrṇapathaka-pattana came on the way of a traveller from Vidishā to Mānyakheta (p. 62).
note: A tale in S.M.K. states that Pūrṇapathaka-pattana lay on the way of a traveller from Vidishā to Mānyakheta (p. 62).
author: Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras — Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
quote: Sircar, who was then the Government Epigraphist for India, happened to inspect the stone and realised the importance of the inscription which, as found by him, was devoted neither to a distinguished personage, nor to a king, but to eulogise the Sun-god: and his conclusion that the inscribed stone slab originally belonged to the temple of Bhāilla- or Bhāila-svāmin at the place appears to be quite sound.
note: Sircar concluded that the Sun-god eulogy slab, found at Bhilsā (Vidishā), belonged to the temple of Bhāilla-svāmin.
author: Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras — Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
quote: The name Bhilsā still retains the memory of the Sun-deity, a temple dedicated to whom existed there some time back.
note: The name Bhilsā still retains the memory of the Sun-deity, to whom a temple existed there some time back.
author: Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras — Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
quote: The immediate object of the inscription appears to be to record the construction of a temple of Murāri, probably by king Trailōkyavarman himself or by one of his subordinates, and making some donations to it by him. The date of the record, as given in figures only in the end, is the twelfth tithi of the dark half of Chaitra of the (Vikrama) era 1226.
note: Records construction of a temple of Murāri, probably by king Trailōkyavarman, with donations; date Chaitra vadi 12, Vikrama 1216.
author: Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras — Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
quote: THIS inscription is incised on a rectangular stone slab which is now set up above the door-part of a house in front of the Jaina temple at Vidishā, the principal town of a district in Madhya Pradesh.
note: Trailōkyavarman's inscription slab is set above a house door in front of the Jaina temple at Vidishā; discovered in 1969.
author: Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras — Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
quote: The following three stanzas (4-6) inform us that he (probably the king himself) constructed a temple of Murārī in the boar-incarnation, a temple which was very high and as lustrous as the moon (kumuda-bandhu), and also installed in it images of some other deities with their respective weapons. The place where the temple was constructed is not mentioned in this stanza or the name of the place may have been lost in it: but evidently it was the town of Vidishā itself, as we know from the mention of the river Vētravatī occurring in the next stanza, and more so when we take into account that such a massive stone could not have been brought from a far off place.¹ The seventh stanza again refers to the same person who was the constructor of the temple and states that he endowed it with a garden;² and the following three stanzas contain a poetic description of the temple.
note: Stanzas 4-6 describe a lofty temple of Murārī in boar-incarnation; place evidently Vidishā itself, from mention of river Vētravatī.
author: Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)

quote:
Of Ujjayini and Vidisha, indeed, countless mentions are available in ancient literature. In the various Puranas, the Mahabharata, Buddhist literature, the vast Jain literature, various epics, many prose works, champu works, ancient inscriptions and short lyric poems,

note: Countless mentions of Ujjayinī and Vidisha in Purāṇas, Mahābhārata, Buddhist and Jain literature; a systematic description first in Bāṇabhaṭṭa's Kādambarī.
author: Bhagwatilal Rajpurohit

book_title: King Bhoj and Paramara-period Town Architecture (Raja Bhoj aur Parmarkaleen Nagar Sthapatya) — English translation — Bhagwatilal Rajpurohit
quote: Vidisha is extremely famous and popular in Indian history and tradition, in poetry and in archaeology. Its mentions are found in abundance in the Ramayana and Mahabharata, in the Puranas and belles-lettres, and in Buddhist and Jain literature. Kalidasa displayed special interest in describing Vidisha — in his *Meghaduta* and *Malavikagnimitra*. The whole play *Malavikagnimitra* tells the story of the Shunga-era palaces of Vidisha itself.
note: Vidisha famous in tradition and literature; Malavikagnimitra tells the story of Shunga-era palaces of Vidisha.
author: Bhagwatilal Rajpurohit

book_title: King Bhoj and Paramara-period Town Architecture (Raja Bhoj aur Parmarkaleen Nagar Sthapatya) — English translation — Bhagwatilal Rajpurohit
quote:
From being on the bank of the Vidisha (Bes) river, it was called Vaidisha-nagara, whose corrupted form is called Besnagar today.

There was bustle in these settlements until the close of the Gupta age. Afterwards the centre of the settlement began to shift toward the north of the Betwa, where the settlement of Vidisha is today.
note: Name Besnagar derived from Vaidisha-nagara on the Vidisha (Bes) river; the settlement centre later shifted north of the Betwa.
author: Bhagwatilal Rajpurohit

book_title: King Bhoj and Paramara-period Town Architecture (Raja Bhoj aur Parmarkaleen Nagar Sthapatya) — English translation — Bhagwatilal Rajpurohit
quote: The land of Malava, bounded "Chambal on this side, Betwa on that," is endowed with ancient cultural glory. Even before the Malavas, this land and its towns kept attaining the glory of a capital.¹ Vidisha had already become a capital in the age of the Ramayana itself.
note: Malava bounded 'Chambal on this side, Betwa on that'; Vidisha already a capital in the age of the Ramayana.
author: Bhagwatilal Rajpurohit

book_title: King Bhoj and Paramara-period Town Architecture (Raja Bhoj aur Parmarkaleen Nagar Sthapatya) — English translation — Bhagwatilal Rajpurohit
quote: The ancient name of Bhailasvamipur was Vidisha. In the Ramayana, Mahabharata, various Puranas, the various versions of the *Brihatkatha* and the like, and in the Jataka stories and the vast Jain literature, countless mentions of Vidisha are found. The field of action of Kalidasa's play *Malavikagnimitra* is Vidisha itself, which is described as the capital of the Shungas. In the *Meghaduta* too it is called a "capital," and the pleasure-caves here are described.
note: Ancient name of Bhailasvamipur was Vidisha; mentions in Ramayana, Puranas, Jataka and Jain literature; Malavikagnimitra set in Vidisha, the Shunga capital.
author: Bhagwatilal Rajpurohit

book_title: King Bhoj and Paramara-period Town Architecture (Raja Bhoj aur Parmarkaleen Nagar Sthapatya) — English translation — Bhagwatilal Rajpurohit
quote: For instance, Patanjali's residence Gonarda has now been identified as Godarmau near Bhopal. From Buddhist literature it is clear that this site was a trading centre situated between Vidisha and Ujjayini.
note: Patañjali's residence Gonarda identified as Godarmau near Bhopal; Buddhist literature shows it as a trading centre between Vidisha and Ujjayinī.
author: Bhagwatilal Rajpurohit

book_title: King Bhoj and Paramara-period Town Architecture (Raja Bhoj aur Parmarkaleen Nagar Sthapatya) — English translation — Bhagwatilal Rajpurohit
quote: Bhailasvamidevapura kept the cultural tradition of ancient Vidisha unbroken from the 9th to the 12th century. It was a prosperous centre of the Jain and Vedic religions, and many beautiful and vast temples had been built there, which, according to Muslim historians, invaders such as Iltutmish and Alauddin Khilji later razed to the ground.
note: Bhailasvamidevapura kept Vidisha's tradition unbroken from the 9th to 12th century; a prosperous Jain and Vedic centre with temples razed according to Muslim historians.
author: Bhagwatilal Rajpurohit

book_title: King Bhoj and Paramara-period Town Architecture (Raja Bhoj aur Parmarkaleen Nagar Sthapatya) — English translation — Bhagwatilal Rajpurohit
quote: Vidisha was in truth a town of Vaishyas (merchants), because it was situated on the trade-route (*sartha-patha*) running from Shravasti through Kaushambi to Avanti, and on the routes going thence toward Mathura and toward Vidarbha. Consequently, in ancient times it became a chief centre of trade. This is why there was a vast settlement of wealthy Vaishyas there, which was called Veshnagar.
note: Vidisha as a trade centre on the sartha-patha routes from Shravasti through Kaushambi to Avanti, toward Mathura and Vidarbha.
author: Bhagwatilal Rajpurohit

book_title: Jagta Hua Kasba / कथा उदयपुर — English translation
page: ≈ p. 58 (Hindi original); also at ≈ p. 58 (Hindi original)
quote: Vidisha was a larger and more ancient city than Udaipur, whose known history comfortably takes [one] up to the Mauryas. In the Maurya empire, before becoming emperor, Ashoka had lived in Ujjain. The stupas of Sanchi, near Vidisha, had begun to be built just then. Kalidasa's Meghadutas (cloud-messengers) are seen making the aerial journey of Vidisha. In between, the Gupta period passed, the proofs of which are scattered here and there in this region.
note: Vidisha larger and more ancient than Udaipur; known history to the Mauryas, Sanchi stupas, Kalidasa's Meghaduta, Gupta period remains.

book_title: Jagta Hua Kasba / कथा उदयपुर — English translation
quote: This was a memorable journey of such a city where, two thousand years ago, a Greek ambassador had come. He, coming to Vidisha, had decided — under the influence of the society and customs here — to accept the Vaishnava religion. That is an immortal episode, worthy of pride for the Vidisha recorded in history, the memory of which is recorded in a stone pillar on the bank of the Betwa river. That pillar is famous by the name of Khamba Baba, which must once have been erected, in the form of a flag-pillar (*garud-stambha*), in front of a temple. Today no trace of the temple remains. But that inscription of Heliodorus can still be read on that pillar today.
note: A Greek ambassador adopted the Vaishnava religion at Vidisha; recorded on a stone pillar by the Betwa, Khamba Baba, once a garuda-stambha; the Heliodorus inscription can still be read.

book_title: Jagta Hua Kasba / कथा उदयपुर — English translation
quote: He too lost his heart to Vidisha — so much that he changed his very religion. He had the formal declaration of it inscribed upon a large pillar, so that history might know it well. Seeing that pillar on the banks of the Vetravati (Betwa), that whole era revolved in Heliodorus's eyes — when his glittering chariots had reached here via Mathura.
note: Heliodorus changed his religion and had the declaration inscribed on a large pillar on the bank of the Vetravati (Betwa); literary retelling.

book_title: Jagta Hua Kasba / कथा उदयपुर — English translation
quote: When he had come here for the first time, the tales of the Magadha emperor Ashoka and of Pushyamitra Shunga were very fresh. The construction of the stupas at Sanchi was going on.
note: At Heliodorus's first coming the tales of Ashoka and Pushyamitra Shunga were fresh and the Sanchi stupas were under construction.

book_title: Jagta Hua Kasba / कथा उदयपुर — English translation
quote:
Today's Malwa, in the centuries before Christ, was known by two names — Dasharna and Avanti. This vast region was, collectively, under Ashoka. Later it came to be called Malwa. Vidisha was the centre of eastern Malwa, and Ujjayini of western Malwa.

- Udaipur, about seventy kilometres from Vidisha, cannot even be called a town (*kasba*) today. A sleeping sort of village, that awaits the moment of waking from its past… A thousand years ago from today, when it was in its prime *[the source reads "सुमावस्था," apparently for "सु-अवस्था" — good/flourishing state]*, its splendour would have been that of the temple-city of the ancient Dasharna kingdom.
note: Malwa in centuries before Christ was known as Dasharna and Avanti; Vidisha centre of eastern Malwa; Udaipur about 70 km from Vidisha, in its prime perhaps the temple-city of the ancient Dasharna kingdom.

book_title: Jagta Hua Kasba / कथा उदयपुर — English translation
quote: Vishnu stands, in his majestic posture, hand on hip, splendidly, in the Varaha (boar) incarnation. The Earth, in the form of a woman, is on his tusk. Vishnu has rescued the Earth drowned in the deluge. He is gazing, unblinking, at this hope-giving scene of his adored Vishnu. In Udayagiri, the 1500-year-old sacred sign of the Gupta emperors, inscribed on stone. The episode of Chandragupta and Dhruvaswamini has come alive.
note: Varaha image on the rock at Udayagiri; 1500-year-old Gupta inscription; Chandragupta and Dhruvaswamini episode.

book_title: Jagta Hua Kasba / कथा उदयपुर — English translation
quote: Once I happened to visit a place that lies about 15 kilometres from Udaipur, toward Patari, amid scenic, verdant hills. If you join Udaipur to Patari on Google Maps, this place is exactly in the middle. From the ruins of Patari it is plainly evident that it must have been a developed town in the time of the Mauryas and the Gupta kings.
note: Place about 15 km from Udaipur toward Patari; ruins of Patari show it must have been a developed town in Mauryan and Gupta times (author's reading).

book_title: Temples of India
quote: Two other temples of a comparable date existed, one dedicated to Sankarshana and Vasudeva at Nagari (ancient Madhyamika) in Udaipur District, Rajasthan and the other, also a Bhagavata (Vaishnava) shrine, at Besnagar near Sanchi in Central India. Both of them were elliptical on plan and were possibly made of timber, but their remains are too scrappy to yield an idea of their elevation and design. In front of the Besnagar shrine stands the famous stone pillar recording that this Garuda-standard was set up … by the Greek ambassador Heliodorus who proudly called himself a Bhagavata (Vaishnava).
note: A Bhagavata shrine at Besnagar near Sanchi, elliptical on plan and possibly of timber; in front stands the pillar of the Greek ambassador Heliodorus, who called himself a Bhagavata.

book_title: Temples of India
quote: Small, flat-roofed shrines comprising a tri-ratha sanctum and a portico with two pillars in front are found in Central India, continuing the tradition of the early Gupta temple form. More than a dozen of them have been recently discovered at the sites of Ramgarh, Chhapara and Badoh in District Vidisha, near Sanchi, in addition to a few from the Lalitpur area of District Jhansi. These are unpretentious temples with a simple podium, a wall of large slabs, and a flat monolithic slab-roof each for the sanctum and the portico, the latter being slightly lower. Most of them are smaller than the earliest Gupta temples at Sanchi and Tigawa and are generally simpler in construction, though they have a more ornate door-frame and pillars,
note: More than a dozen small flat-roofed Gupta-tradition shrines recently discovered at Ramgarh, Chhapara and Badoh in District Vidisha, near Sanchi.

book_title: Temples of India
quote: The above temples are followed by the Jarai Math at Barwasagar (District Jhansi), and Gadarimal Temple at Badoh (District Vidisha).
note: Names the Gadarimal Temple at Badoh (District Vidisha) among Pratihara-period temples, with the Jarai Math at Barwasagar.

book_title: The Hindu Temple, Volume I — Stella Kramrisch
quote: Lithic in its construction and not only in its substance is the solid stone fence unearthed in Besnagar, Bhopal. It belonged to an “Uttama Prāsāda” of Vāsudeva—only its brick foundation exists—of which also the Garudā stone pillar with the inscription of Heliodoros, son of Dion and an inhabitant of Taxila, formed part (see also ASIAR, 1913-14, Pt. I.). These relics date from the 2nd century B.C.
note: Besnagar (Bhopal): a solid stone fence belonged to an 'Uttama Prasada' of Vasudeva, only its brick foundation surviving, of which the Garuda pillar with Heliodoros's inscription formed part; the relics date from the 2nd century BC.
author: Stella Kramrisch

book_title: The Hindu Temple, Volume I — Stella Kramrisch
quote: The earliest preserved dry masonry is the stone facing of Stūpa I, Sañcī; the earliest occurrence of lime mortar in historical times is in the brick foundation of the Viṣṇu temple at Besnagar (ASIAR, 1913-14).
note: Earliest preserved dry masonry is the stone facing of Stupa I, Sanchi; earliest historical occurrence of lime mortar is the brick foundation of the Vishnu temple at Besnagar (ASIAR 1913-14).
author: Stella Kramrisch

book_title: The Skanda-Purāṇa, Part XIII
quote: It was due to the service to Khaṇḍeśvara that a maidservant and her husband of Vaishya community of Vidiśā were born as Queen Kāntimati and King Bhadrāśva.
note: Editorial note on the Skanda Purana Khandesvara legend: a maidservant and her husband of the Vaishya community of Vidisa are reborn as Queen Kantimati and King Bhadrashva. Names Vidisa in a puranic tale; not historical evidence.

book_title: The Skanda-Purāṇa, Part XIII
quote: This your queen was a maidservant of a Vaisya named Haridatta in the city of Vaidisā. You were her husband. As a result of the incomplete Vrata you became a servant. That Vaisya went to Mahākāla and worshipped Lord Maheśvara duly with splendid scents, flowers, etc. After worshipping, he returned home where both of you were the supervisors.
note: In the same Skanda Purana legend the queen was formerly a maidservant of the Vaisya Haridatta in the city of Vaidisa, who worshipped Mahakala; a legendary reference to the city, not historical evidence.

book_title: The Temple Architecture of India — Adam Hardy
quote: Early in the 5th century, at Udayagiri near Vidisha (MP) and at Ramgarh in the same region, the Gupta rulers initiated the creation of Brahminical or Hindu cave temples, along with sculpted panels establishing long-lasting formulations for Hindu iconography.
note: Early in the 5th century at Udayagiri near Vidisha and Ramgarh, Gupta rulers initiated Brahminical cave temples with sculpted panels.
author: Adam Hardy

book_title: The Hindu Temple, Volume II — Stella Kramrisch
quote: \( ^{184} \)  On a structural pillar at Besnagar, see P. Brown, op. cit.
note: Footnote locates an āmalaka carved above the railing of a casket on a structural pillar at Besnagar (P. Brown).
author: Stella Kramrisch

book_title: The Cultural Heritage of Madhya Bharat — Patil, D. R.
quote: Whatever be the truth behind this tradition it is certain, in the 6th century B. C., in the time of the Buddha, Mahishmati's fame as an important city and centre of trade was well established. With the emergence of Ujjain as a great city in subsequent times the importance of Mahishmati receded into back-ground though we do hear about the town as late as the 5th century A. D.
note: Mahishmati an important city and centre of trade by the Buddha's time, receding as Ujjain rose; regional trade-centre background.
author: Patil, D. R.

book_title: The Cultural Heritage of Madhya Bharat — Patil, D. R.
quote: In historical times Nemawar fell on the trade route from the north to the Deccan since it is mentioned as such by Albiruni in the early 11th century A. D.
note: Nemawar lay on the trade route from the north to the Deccan, mentioned by Albiruni in the early 11th century A.D.
author: Patil, D. R.

book_title: कथा उदयपुर (Jagta Hua Kasba) — Hindi original
quote:
आठवीं सदी में पाल, प्रतिहार और राष्ट्रकूट राजवंशों के बीच चले त्रिपक्षीय संघर्ष के बाद के दौर में उत्तर एवं दक्षिण भारत में बड़े सियासी बदलाव हुए। कुछ नए राजवंश उभरकर सामने आए, जिन्होंने इतिहास में अपनी शानदार मौजूदगी दर्ज कराई। इनमें सबसे खास थे दक्षिण में कल्याणी के चालुक्य, जो वातापी के चालुक्य वंश के उत्तराधिकारी थे।
*Gloss [my translation]:* After the tripartite struggle among the Pala, Pratihara and Rashtrakuta dynasties in the eighth century, there were big political changes in north and south India. Some new dynasties emerged and recorded their splendid presence in history. Most notable among them in the south were the Chalukyas of Kalyani, successors of the Chalukya dynasty of Vatapi.
note: Background: political change after the 8th-century tripartite struggle of Pala, Pratihara and Rashtrakuta; new dynasties emerged, notably the Chalukyas of Kalyani.
gloss: After the tripartite struggle among the Pala, Pratihara and Rashtrakuta dynasties in the eighth century, there were big political changes in north and south India. Some new dynasties emerged and recorded their splendid presence in history. Most notable among them in the south were the Chalukyas of Kalyani, successors of the Chalukya dynasty of Vatapi.

book_title: कथा उदयपुर (Jagta Hua Kasba) — Hindi original
quote:
प्रतिहारों की ताकत कमजोर होने पर तीन ताकतें उभरकर आईं। इनमें कलचुरी के चेदि, जैजाकभुक्ति के चंदेल और मालवा के परमार एक साथ क्षितिज पर उगते हैं।
*Gloss [my translation]:* When the Pratiharas' strength weakened, three powers emerged. Among them the Chedis of the Kalachuris, the Chandellas of Jejakabhukti and the Paramaras of Malwa rise on the horizon together.
note: With the Pratihara decline three powers rose together: Chedi of the Kalachuris, Chandellas of Jejakabhukti and Paramaras of Malwa.
gloss: When the Pratiharas' strength weakened, three powers emerged. Among them the Chedis of the Kalachuris, the Chandellas of Jejakabhukti and the Paramaras of Malwa rise on the horizon together.

book_title: कथा उदयपुर (Jagta Hua Kasba) — Hindi original
quote:
मुरादपुर से लेकर सोनारी तक विष्णु की प्रतिमाओं का पाया जाना इतिहास के सिरों को परमारों से भी पीछे गुप्त शासकों से जोड़ता है जो विष्णु के उपासक थे। इससे हम अंदाजा लगा सकते हैं कि उदयादित्य से पाँच सौ साल पहले भी यहाँ स्थापत्य के

चमत्कार रचने की प्रक्रिया निरंतर थी।
*Gloss [my translation]:* The finding of Vishnu images from Muradpur to Sonari connects the threads of history to the Gupta rulers, who were worshippers of Vishnu, even further back than the Paramaras. From this we can guess that even five hundred years before Udayaditya the process of creating wonders of architecture was continuous here.
note: Author infers from Vishnu images found from Muradpur to Sonari a link to Gupta rulers, Vishnu worshippers, and building activity five hundred years before Udayaditya (author's inference).
gloss: The finding of Vishnu images from Muradpur to Sonari connects the threads of history to the Gupta rulers, who were worshippers of Vishnu, even further back than the Paramaras. From this we can guess that even five hundred years before Udayaditya the process of creating wonders of architecture was continuous here.

book_title: कथा उदयपुर (Jagta Hua Kasba) — Hindi original
quote:
उत्तरापथ से दक्षिणापथ को जोड़ने वाला वह पथ मात्र परिवहन का राजमार्ग नहीं बल्कि भक्ति का महामार्ग था जिस पर चेर, चोल, पाण्ड्य, चालुक्य, राष्ट्रकूट आदि विभिन्न राजवंशों ने भारतीय सनातन संस्कृति को अक्षुण्ण रखने के निमित्त न जाने कितनी देव-नगरियाँ, पुरियाँ निर्मित कराईं। जहाँ से भक्ति की धारा जनमानस को चतुर्दिक दीप करती थी।

- यह वही महामार्ग था जिससे होकर ‘द्राविड़ ऊपजी’ भक्तिधारा ने उत्तर भारत में एक से बढ़ कर एक दीपस्तम्भ जगमगा दिए थे। ऐसा ही एक जागृत दीपस्तम्भ था उदयपुर का उदयेश्वर महादेव देवालय।
*Gloss [my translation]:* That path joining Uttarapatha to Dakshinapatha was not merely a highway of transport but a great path of devotion, on which various dynasties such as Chera, Chola, Pandya, Chalukya and Rashtrakuta built countless temple-towns and cities to keep Indian eternal culture unbroken. From where the stream of devotion lit up the people on all sides. This was the same great path through which the Dravidian-born stream of devotion lit one beacon after another in north India. One such living beacon was the Udayeshvara Mahadeva temple of Udaypur.
note: Describes the route joining Uttarapatha with Dakshinapatha as a highway of devotion along which dynasties built temple towns, and calls the Udayeshvara Mahadeva temple one such lamp-post.
gloss: That path joining Uttarapatha to Dakshinapatha was not merely a highway of transport but a great path of devotion, on which various dynasties such as Chera, Chola, Pandya, Chalukya and Rashtrakuta built countless temple-towns and cities to keep Indian eternal culture unbroken. From where the stream of devotion lit up the people on all sides. This was the same great path through which the Dravidian-born stream of devotion lit one beacon after another in north India. One such living beacon was the Udayeshvara Mahadeva temple of Udaypur.

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras — Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
quote: Moreover, the name Avanti denoting West Mālwā reminds us of the earlier times (Ākar-āvanti).
note: The name Avanti denoting West Mālwā 'reminds us of the earlier times (Ākar-āvanti)'.
author: Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)

book_title: Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum, Vol. VII, Part 2: Inscriptions of the Paramāras — Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)
quote: As for the localities occurring in the present grant, Banerji called attention to a town named Upēndrapura mentioned in the Rāṇḍod inscription of the Mattamayūra ascetics and observed that it seems to have given its name to the maṇḍala appearing here. \( ^{2} \)  But the place cannot be located. This part of the maṇḍala seems to have been in the south-eastern portion of the Shivpurī District of Madhya Pradesh, just to the west of the Bēwā and around Rāṇḍ.
note: Banerji linked the Upēndrapura-maṇḍala with a town in the Rāṇḍod inscription; editor places it in the south-eastern Shivpurī District just west of the Bētwā, around Rāṇḍ.
author: Trivedi, Harihar Vithal (ed.)

book_title: Jagta Hua Kasba / कथा उदयपुर — English translation
quote: The finding of Vishnu idols from Muradpur all the way to Sonari links the threads of history to the Gupta rulers — who were worshippers of Vishnu — even further back than the Paramaras. From this we can surmise that even five hundred years before Udayadity, the process of fashioning architectural marvels here was continuous.
note: Author says Vishnu idols from Muradpur to Sonari link the region to the Vishnu-worshipping Guptas, five hundred years before Udayadity.

book_title: Jagta Hua Kasba / कथा उदयपुर — English translation
quote:
- Seeing this newly-built, broad, expansive path, made through public cooperation, one feels as though it was just such a broad splendour of the road to the Deccan that, again and again, kindled the greed of the outside invaders.

- That path, connecting the Uttarapath (northern route) to the Dakshinapath (southern route), was not merely a highway of transport but a great highway of devotion (*bhakti*), upon which various dynasties such as the Chera, Chola, Pandya, Chalukya and Rashtrakuta had built who-knows-how-many god-cities and *puris*, for the sake of keeping India's Sanatan culture unbroken — [cities] from which the stream of devotion illuminated the populace on every side.

- This was the very great highway through which the devotion-stream that "arose in the Dravida [land]" (*Dravid upji*) had, in North India, set aglow one beacon-tower brighter than the next. Just such an awakened beacon-tower was the Udayeshvar Mahadev temple of Udaipur.
note: Author likens the new road to the road to the Deccan, linking the Uttarapath and Dakshinapath, a highway of devotion on which dynasties built temple cities.

book_title: Temples of India
quote: A second example of a Maurya temple uncovered by excavations—Temple 40 at Sanchi—has likewise a consistent plan. It was a stone temple on an apsidal plan, enclosed by an ambulatory and raised on a high, rectangular (26.5 mts. × 14 mts.) socle, approached by two flights of steps from diagonally opposite sides. The superstructure, possibly of timber, has disappeared.
note: Temple 40 at Sanchi, a Maurya apsidal stone temple on a high socle with an ambulatory; superstructure possibly timber and lost.

book_title: Temples of India
quote: The earliest group of Gupta temples, dating from 5th century and showing a single-celled sanctum with a shallow portico resting on 4 pillars in front, is represented by Temple 17 at Sanchi (the site of the famous Buddhist Stupa of the 2nd Century B.C.), the Gupta Temple at Tigawa (District Jabalpur), and the Temples at Eran (District Sagar). A notable feature of these temples is the wider intercolumniation of the pillars in the middle than on the sides. As suggested by the flat roof, square or rectangular in form, the plain treatment of the walls and modestness of size, these temples must obviously have been derived from rock-cut proto-types of which early Gupta examples occur at Udaigiri near Sanchi. In fact Cave-shrine 1 at Udaigiri with a partly rock-cut sanctum and a structural porch of 4 pillars is of the early Gupta type, supporting the aforementioned inference.
note: Earliest Gupta temples at Sanchi (Temple 17), Tigawa and Eran; derived from rock-cut prototypes such as Cave-shrine 1 at Udaigiri near Sanchi.

book_title: Temples of India
quote: As these regions were largely under the sway of the Gurjara-Pratiharas during the 8th and 9th centuries, we may call this style Pratihara. Since the Pratiharas ruled over an extensive empire from Kanauj, the style spread over vast tracts of North India, including the present States of Uttar Pradesh and the Punjab as far as the Himalayas and had its reverberations further east and west.
note: Central India and Rajasthan were largely under the Gurjara-Pratiharas in the 8th and 9th centuries, who ruled from Kanauj; hence the style is called Pratihara.

book_title: Temples of India
quote: Both have elaborately ornamented pillars and entrance door-frame of five bands, but while the Jarai Math is an unpretentious structure comprising only a sanctum and a vestibule, the Gadarmal Temple adds to these a mandapa with transepts and a porch enclosed by a high balustrade punctuated with projecting elephant heads. The Gadarmal Temple stands on an ample, ornate platform surrounded by seven subsidiary shrines and has lavishly decorated mandapa pillars and is a little more evolved on plan and in design than the foregoing Pratihara temples.
note: Gadarmal Temple: mandapa with transepts, a porch with a balustrade of elephant heads, on an ornate platform surrounded by seven subsidiary shrines.

book_title: Temples of India
quote: The Chandellas of Jejakabhukti who supplanted the Imperial Pratiharas of Kanauj, the Kalachuris of Dahala and the Paramaras of Malwa were mighty powers which administered parts of this region simultaneously and competed with one another in the arts of war and peace. There were also lesser dynasties such as the Kachchhapaghatas of Narwar, Dubkund and Gwalior. These powers vied with one another in building temples with which Central India was once thickly studded, but of which only a small fraction has survived the ravages of man and nature. The rich traditions of Gupta art and architecture were kept up by the Pratiharas whose monumental remains in this region have already been noticed in a previous chapter. Between the 10th and 12th centuries the Kalachuris kept the torch burning in the eastern part of Central India, the Chandellas in the central part, the Paramaras largely in the western part and the Kachchhapaghatas mainly in the northern part.
note: Chandellas, Kalachuris and Paramaras as mighty powers of Central India; Paramaras largely in the western part between the 10th and 12th centuries.

book_title: The Hindu Temple, Volume I — Stella Kramrisch
quote: Here are some of the earliest inscriptions: On a Garuḍa pillar from Bhilsa, an ‘uttama Prāśada, of Bhagavat, 2nd century B.C., J. N.
note: Earliest inscriptions using Prāśāda for a temple include a Garuḍa pillar from Bhilsa naming an uttama Prāśada of Bhagavat, 2nd century B.C.
author: Stella Kramrisch

book_title: The Hindu Temple, Volume I — Stella Kramrisch
quote: Brāhmanical worship cut its entry into the rock. It has the shape of a small, flat roofed Garbhagrha. To it is added, as in the contemporary Gupta temples, a structural porch or manḍapam (Udayagiri, Bhopal, C. I.).
note: About 400 A.D. Brāhmanical worship cut into rock at Udayagiri, Bhopal: small flat-roofed Garbhagṛha with structural porch
author: Stella Kramrisch

book_title: The Hindu Temple, Volume I — Stella Kramrisch
quote: 99 This earliest Brāhmaṇical rock-cut temple is amongst the earliest fully preserved Brāhmaṇical shrines. It dates from the reign of Candragupta II, 382-401 A.D. (Cunningham, ASR, Vol. X, p. 41).
note: Earliest Brāhmaṇical rock-cut temple at Udayagiri dates from Candragupta II, 382-401 A.D.
author: Stella Kramrisch

book_title: The Hindu Temple, Volume I — Stella Kramrisch
quote:
The places of pilgrimage are distributed through the entire country and are called Tirtha and Kṣetra. The number of these sacred sites is large; the 'Mahābhārata' speaks of hundreds of places of pilgrimage.\( ^{2} \)
Tīrtha is the name of a place of pilgrimage on the bank of a river, the sea-shore or a lake.
note: General account of Tirthas and Kṣetras as places of pilgrimage distributed through the country, tīrtha being a river-bank, sea-shore or lake site.
author: Stella Kramrisch

book_title: The Hindu Temple, Volume I — Stella Kramrisch
quote: Heretics, such as the Buddhists and Jains enlarged and embellished those retreats into rock cut monasteries and temples. The Hindus too carved and hollowed the living rock into cave temples though with some reticence, the earliest cave sanctuary, in Udayagiri in Central India dates from about 400 A.D. only.
note: Hindu rock-cut sanctuaries came with reticence; the earliest cave sanctuary, at Udayagiri in Central India, dates from about 400 AD.
author: Stella Kramrisch

book_title: The Temple Architecture of India — Adam Hardy
quote:
Early stupas were raised to encase relics of the Buddha or of a disciple or a saint, and thus radiated miraculous power.\(^{1}\) The great stupas of peninsular India, originally surrounded by thriving monastic complexes, belong to the period between the 2nd century BC and the 3rd century AD (7.1).
7.1 The Great Stupa (Stupa 1), Sanchi (MP), c 1st century BC, probably built over an earlier structure, which would have encased a sacred relic.
note: Great stupas of the period between the 2nd century BC and 3rd century AD; Great Stupa (Stupa 1), Sanchi (MP), c 1st century BC.
author: Adam Hardy

book_title: History of the Paramāra Dynasty — Ganguly, D. C.
quote: About this time the Candellas of Jejâkabhukti extended their territory up to Bhilsa on the west. The Khajuraho inscription, dated 954 A. D., registers \( ^{4} \) the fact that at this time the Candella kingdom extended as far as Bhâsvat (Bhilsa), which was situated on the bank of the river Mâlava.
note: Candella kingdom extended to Bhilsa (Bhāsvat) on the Mālava river by the Khajuraho inscription of 954 A.D.
author: Ganguly, D. C.

book_title: Temple Economics (Arthavyavasthā of Mandirs), Volume I — Singh, Sandeep
quote: Remnants of a Mauryan-era, brick-and-stone structure believed to be a mandir have been excavated in Baiarat district in Rajasthan and dated to the 3rd century BCE, and a similar oval, brick temple plan has been excavated at Besnagar, Vidisha, Madhya Pradesh dated to the 2nd Century BCE.
note: Cites an oval, brick temple plan excavated at Besnagar, Vidisha, dated to the 2nd century BCE (secondary summary in a temple-economics book).
author: Singh, Sandeep
